groups.passage:
A Training Session for Different Players

A local sports club introduced a weekly indoor session for people with different levels of physical mobility. Its coach initially planned to have everyone complete the same set of activities in the same order. During the first session, however, she noticed that some players could perform a passing exercise comfortably while others found the distance between partners difficult. The exercise was intended to develop control of the ball, rather than to test how far each player could throw.

The coach marked three possible distances on the floor. Players chose a starting distance and could move further apart when they felt ready. She also offered balls of different weights, while keeping the central aim of the exercise the same.

At the end of each session, players recorded their own progress and suggested adjustments for the following week. Some preferred a greater challenge, while others valued the chance to practise a skill at a steady pace. The coach used these comments to plan activities with several levels of difficulty. She found that players spent less time waiting for individual instructions and more time practising.

questions.question_text: What problem did the coach observe during the first session?

options.text: The passing distance was difficult for some players.
The players could not find the indoor sports hall.
All the balls were too heavy for every player.
There were not enough partners to form pairs.

questions.question_text: What was the original aim of the passing exercise?

options.text: To compare the weight of different balls.
To select players for a competition.
To measure the longest possible throw.

questions.question_text: How did the coach modify the exercise?

options.text: She removed all passing activities from the session.
She assigned a single permanent distance to each pair.
She offered several passing distances and ball weights.
She required every player to throw from the longest distance.

questions.question_text: What did players do at the end of each session?

options.text: They recorded progress and proposed changes.
They took a written test on sports rules.
They ranked each other by throwing distance.
They chose a different coach for the next session.

questions.question_text: Why did the coach retain the central aim while varying the equipment and distance?

options.text: The club needed to avoid keeping records of individual progress.
Players could practise the same skill at a suitable level.
Players were being assessed only on equipment selection.
The coach wanted all players to reach exactly the same distance immediately.

questions.question_text: Which statement best summarises the passage?

options.text: Identical exercises are necessary to make group training fair.
Flexible practice arrangements can support a shared learning goal.
The club's greatest challenge was finding a suitable indoor venue.
Players learn best when individual feedback is discouraged.

groups.passage:
The Journey of a Reusable Crate

A small group of vegetable suppliers introduced reusable plastic crates for deliveries to local shops. Previously, each delivery arrived in cardboard boxes that the shops had to dispose of. Under the new scheme, suppliers collected empty crates when they made their next scheduled delivery. Each crate carried a code identifying the supplier responsible for it.

Although the system reduced the amount of cardboard used, it soon created an unexpected problem. Some shops received deliveries from several suppliers, and empty crates were occasionally returned to the wrong one. The suppliers agreed to establish a shared sorting point. Drivers could return any participating crate to this point, where staff scanned its code and assigned it to the correct supplier.

The suppliers also monitored the number of trips each crate completed before it needed replacement. They wanted to know whether the additional transport and cleaning involved in the scheme were justified by repeated use. When a shop suggested buying more crates to solve a temporary shortage, the group first examined where existing crates were being held. They discovered that many were waiting at the sorting point because collection times had not been coordinated. Adjusting the timetable improved availability without an immediate purchase.

questions.question_text: How were empty crates originally collected under the new scheme?

options.text: By customers bringing them to vegetable farms.
By shops sending them through the postal service.
Through a separate collection service every evening.
During the suppliers' next scheduled deliveries.

questions.question_text: What was the purpose of the code on each crate?

options.text: To show the customer's payment method.
To record the shop's opening hours.
To indicate the weight of vegetables inside.
To identify the supplier responsible for the crate.

questions.question_text: Why was a shared sorting point introduced?

options.text: Cardboard boxes had become cheaper than plastic crates.
Shops wanted to stop receiving vegetables altogether.
Drivers had been prohibited from making scheduled deliveries.
Crates were sometimes returned to the wrong supplier.

questions.question_text: Why did the suppliers track the number of trips made by each crate?

options.text: To require replacement after every delivery.
To assess whether repeated use justified the extra transport and cleaning.
To calculate the weight of each load of cardboard.
To decide which shops sold the largest amount of vegetables.

questions.question_text: The word coordinated in the final paragraph is closest in meaning to -------.
What lesson can be drawn from the temporary shortage?

options.text: Buying more crates always reduces the need for coordination.
A shared sorting point makes reusable crates unsuitable for deliveries.
Poor circulation of existing crates can resemble a shortage of equipment.
Increasing the number of crates necessarily increases shop sales.

groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
When an Animal Changes Its Routine

A wildlife research group was investigating whether animals in a protected area changed their activity in response to human presence. Motion-sensitive cameras had recorded that a small mammal was more active at night near a frequently used walking trail than in a quieter part of the reserve. The researchers wondered whether the animal was avoiding people. However, the two areas differed in several other respects, including vegetation, shelter and the availability of food.

To explore the question further, the group selected several pairs of observation sites with similar vegetation and shelter. Within each pair, one site was relatively close to a trail and the other was further away. Cameras were placed at the same height and operated during the same weeks. The team also used counters to record the number of people passing each trail, because a path shown on a map might be rarely visited in practice.

The observations revealed that the difference in animal activity was most marked near trails with many visitors. Yet the pattern was weaker during weeks when a particular kind of fruit became available at both locations. The researchers considered that food availability might partly influence how the animals used the sites. They did not assume that the presence of people was irrelevant, but they recognised that the animals could be responding to more than one factor.

The group proposed collecting data in another season and recording the availability of food more systematically. It also recommended keeping the existing camera positions so that observations could be compared over time. The study demonstrates the value of examining competing explanations before attributing a behavioural change to a single cause.

questions.question_text: What did the initial camera recordings show?

options.text: The mammal spent all its time beside the trail during the day.
The mammal never visited either part of the reserve.
The mammal was more active at night near the frequently used trail.
The mammal was equally active at every site.

questions.question_text: Why could the initial difference not be confidently explained by human presence alone?

options.text: The two areas also differed in habitat and food availability.
The reserve contained no trails that people actually used.
The cameras had recorded only photographs of visitors.
The researchers had already proven that visitors never affected the mammal.

questions.question_text: Why did the researchers select pairs of sites with similar vegetation and shelter?

options.text: To attract mammals to the most frequently used trails.
To make the fruit grow at exactly the same rate.
To ensure every camera recorded the same individual animal.
To reduce the influence of habitat differences on the comparison.

questions.question_text: What was the reason for installing counters along the trails?

options.text: To measure the amount of fruit eaten by mammals.
To measure actual visitor numbers instead of relying on the existence of paths.
To control the height at which cameras were installed.
To determine how many walking routes appeared on maps.

questions.question_text: The word marked in the third paragraph is closest in meaning to -------.
When was the difference in animal activity weaker?

options.text: When all cameras were moved to new locations.
During weeks when a certain fruit was available at both sites.
During weeks when the reserve had no food at any site.
When every trail was crowded with visitors.

questions.question_text: Why did the team recommend keeping the camera positions unchanged?

options.text: To make systematic food records unnecessary.
To make observations from different periods more comparable.
To avoid collecting information about seasonal changes.
To guarantee that all animals followed identical routines.

questions.question_text: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?

options.text: Human visitors are the sole cause of changes in animal behaviour in protected areas.
Several environmental influences should be examined before explaining a change in animal activity.
Food availability makes research into human disturbance unnecessary.
Camera placement alone can establish what motivates an animal's routine.
